title: Bash & Python
description: The daily 30 minute companion of the DevOps roadmap.

tasks.title: Create a file called hello.sh and write two echo lines in it.
Run it with bash hello.sh and confirm both lines print.
Add a comment line starting with a hash and confirm it does not run.
Add a shebang line at the top so the system knows which interpreter to use.
Make the script executable with chmod and run it directly with a dot slash.
Work out why you need the dot slash and write the reason in your notes.
Create three variables and print them with echo. Notice there are no spaces around the equals sign.
Print a variable inside double quotes and inside single quotes. Explain the difference.
Write a script that creates a folder whose name comes from a variable.
Capture the output of the date command into a variable and print it.
Build a timestamped filename using command substitution.
Write a script that greets the current user by name using whoami.
Use read to ask the user for their name, then greet them.
Add a prompt message so the user knows what to type.
Write a script that asks for a folder name and creates it.
Read the first argument passed to your script and print it.
Handle two arguments, and print how many were given using the count variable.
Rewrite yesterday's script so the folder name comes from an argument instead of a prompt.
Run a command that works and one that fails, checking the exit status after each.
Add an exit line to your script with a non zero number and confirm the status matches.
Write down why exit codes matter for scripts that run automatically.
Write an if statement that checks whether a file exists before touching it.
Add an else branch that prints a message when the file is missing.
Add a check at the top of a script that exits early if no argument was given.
Learn the tests for file exists, directory exists and file is readable, then use all three.
Compare two strings for equal and not equal inside an if statement.
Check whether a variable is empty and handle that case properly.
Compare two numbers using the numeric operators for greater than and less than.
Do simple arithmetic in a script and print the result.
Write a script that counts files in a folder and warns if there are more than ten.
Loop over a list of words and print each one.
Loop over every file in a directory and print its name.
Write a loop that adds a suffix to every text file in a test folder.
Loop over files in a folder and print each one with its permissions.
Write a script that lists only the files that are writable by you.
Write a script that sets 644 on every file inside a folder you choose.
Write a while loop that counts from one to five.
Read a text file line by line with a while loop and print each line numbered.
Add a break so the loop stops early when it meets a chosen word.
Write a case statement that responds differently to three different arguments.
Build a small menu script that offers three actions and runs the chosen one.
Add a default branch that handles anything unexpected.
Make a script write its output to a log file instead of the screen.
Change it so each run appends to the log with a timestamp rather than overwriting.
Send error messages to a separate file from the normal output.
Write a script that checks whether a named process is running.
Extend it so it starts the process only if it is not already running.
Print the process id of a running program from inside your script.
Start a long command in the background from a script and carry on.
Use wait so the script pauses until the background job finishes.
Run three commands in parallel from one script and wait for all of them.
Write a script that reports whether nginx is active, using systemctl inside an if.
Extend it to restart the service only when it is not running.
Make the script print a clear one line result that a human can read at a glance.
Write a script that searches a log file for a word you pass as an argument.
Extend it to count how many matches it found and print the number.
Make it print a warning when the count goes above a number you choose.
Write a script that checks whether a package is installed.
Extend it to install the package only when it is missing.
Loop over a list of five packages and report the status of each one.
Write a script that prints disk usage as a percentage number only.
Make it warn when usage passes a threshold you set.
Write a script that prints the five largest folders in a path you pass in.
Write a script that tars a folder into a timestamped archive.
Add a check that exits with a clear message if the source folder does not exist.
Extend it to delete archives older than seven days.
Read an environment variable inside a script and use it.
Give the variable a default value for when it is not set.
Move your script settings into a separate config file and source it.
Put your backup script into cron and confirm it runs.
Fix the script so it works under cron by using full paths everywhere.
Make the cron job write a line to a log every time it runs.
Add set with the e and u flags and observe how the script now fails fast.
Put quotes around every variable and test with a filename containing a space.
Install shellcheck, run it on your scripts, and fix every warning it reports.

days.title: Build One Tool You Will Keep

tasks.title: Choose one small job you did by hand this month and turn it into a script.
Write it with argument handling, a usage message, error checks and quoting.
Run shellcheck until it reports nothing.
Commit it to the GitHub repository you created on day 26 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What is a shebang line?
options: The first line saying which interpreter runs the script
questions.explanation: It tells the system which program should execute the file.

questions.prompt: Why do you need dot slash to run a script in the current folder?
options: Because the current directory is not in your PATH
questions.explanation: The shell only searches PATH, so you must give an explicit path for a local file.

questions.prompt: Which command makes a script executable?
questions.explanation: chmod changes the permission bits, and you need the execute bit set.

questions.prompt: How do you assign a variable in bash?
questions.explanation: There must be no spaces around the equals sign.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between double and single quotes?
options: Double quotes expand variables, single quotes do not
questions.explanation: Single quotes take the text literally, which is sometimes exactly what you want.

questions.prompt: What does command substitution do?
options: Captures a command's output into a variable
Runs a command in the background
questions.explanation: It lets you use the result of one command as a value inside your script.

questions.prompt: Which command reads input from the user into a variable?
questions.explanation: read pauses the script and stores what the user types.

questions.prompt: How do you write a comment in bash?
options: A hash at the start of the line
questions.explanation: Everything after the hash on that line is ignored.

questions.prompt: What character starts a variable when you use its value?
questions.explanation: The dollar sign tells the shell to substitute the variable's value.

questions.prompt: Why build a timestamped filename?
options: So each run creates a separate file instead of overwriting
questions.explanation: Timestamps stop each run from destroying the previous result.

questions.prompt: What does echo do?
options: Prints text or a variable value
questions.explanation: It is the simplest way to see what your script is doing.

questions.prompt: Where should the shebang line appear?
questions.explanation: It only works as the first line of the file.

questions.prompt: A script with the execute permission removed can still be run with bash filename.
questions.explanation: Calling bash directly bypasses the need for the execute bit on the file.

questions.prompt: Putting spaces around the equals sign when assigning a variable causes an error.
questions.explanation: Bash reads it as a command with arguments instead of an assignment.

questions.prompt: Writing a small script every day is more useful than reading about bash for an hour.
questions.explanation: Scripting is muscle memory, and it only builds through repetition at the keyboard.

questions.prompt: How do you read the first argument passed to a script?
questions.explanation: Dollar zero holds the script name, and the arguments start at one.

questions.prompt: What does the argument count variable tell you?
questions.explanation: It lets you check the user gave you what the script needs.

questions.prompt: What does an exit code of zero mean?
questions.explanation: Zero means success, and any other number signals a specific failure.

questions.prompt: Why do exit codes matter for automated scripts?
options: Because cron and pipelines use them to decide whether something worked
questions.explanation: Automation has no human watching, so the exit code is how failure is detected.

questions.prompt: Which test checks that a file exists?
questions.explanation: Checking before acting is what stops a script failing halfway through.

questions.prompt: Why check a variable is not empty before using it?
options: Because an empty value can make a command do something destructive
questions.explanation: An empty variable in a delete command is one of the classic ways scripts cause damage.

questions.prompt: What is a guard clause at the top of a script?
options: An early check that exits if the inputs are wrong
questions.explanation: Failing early with a clear message is better than failing later in a confusing way.

questions.prompt: Which comparison would you use for two numbers?
questions.explanation: String and numeric comparison use different operators in bash.

questions.prompt: What does an else branch do?
options: Runs when the if condition is false
questions.explanation: It handles the other case so the script does not silently do nothing.

questions.prompt: Why print a clear message when a check fails?
options: So whoever runs it knows what went wrong and what to fix
questions.explanation: A script that fails silently wastes far more time than one that explains itself.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of a script that assumes its arguments are correct?
options: It can act on the wrong target and cause damage
questions.explanation: Validation is what stands between a typo and a deleted folder.

questions.prompt: When would you exit with a non zero code?
questions.explanation: It is how your script tells the outside world it failed.

questions.prompt: Checking whether a file exists before acting on it makes a script more reliable.
questions.explanation: It replaces an ugly crash with a clear, handled outcome.

questions.prompt: String comparison and numeric comparison use the same operators in bash.
questions.explanation: They use different operators, and mixing them is a common source of confusing bugs.

questions.prompt: A script that exits with zero after failing is a problem for automation.
questions.explanation: Anything running it will believe the work succeeded and carry on.

questions.prompt: What does a for loop do?
options: Repeats until a condition is false
Runs the same steps for each item in a list
questions.explanation: You give it a list and it works through it one item at a time.

questions.prompt: How would you act on every file in a directory?
options: A for loop over the files
questions.explanation: Looping over files is one of the most common things a script does.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a for loop and a while loop?
options: for works through a known list, while repeats until a condition changes
questions.explanation: Use for when you know the items, and while when you are waiting on a condition.

questions.prompt: How do you read a file line by line?
options: A for loop over the filename
questions.explanation: The while and read combination handles each line safely.

questions.prompt: What does break do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: It leaves the loop entirely and continues after it.

questions.prompt: When is a case statement clearer than a chain of if statements?
options: When comparing one value against several possible options
questions.explanation: It reads far better than four or five else branches.

questions.prompt: Why add a default branch to a case statement?
options: To handle input you did not expect
questions.explanation: Unexpected input is guaranteed eventually, and silence is the worst response.

questions.prompt: How do you make a script write output to a file instead of the screen?
options: Redirect the output with the greater than sign
questions.explanation: This is the same redirection you learned on day 9 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: How do you add to a log file without erasing it?
questions.explanation: One overwrites and two append, and getting this wrong destroys log history.

questions.prompt: Why send errors to a separate file from normal output?
options: So problems are easy to find instead of buried in normal output
questions.explanation: Separating the streams is what makes an unattended script debuggable.

questions.prompt: Why timestamp each line written to a log?
options: So you know when each run happened
questions.explanation: A log with no times cannot answer the question of when something broke.

questions.prompt: What should a loop that renames files do first?
options: Test on a copy or a test folder
questions.explanation: A loop applies your mistake to every file at once, so test first.

questions.prompt: A loop with a mistake in it will make that mistake once per item.
questions.explanation: That multiplying effect is exactly why you test loops on throwaway data first.

questions.prompt: The redirection you learned in the Linux track works the same way inside scripts.
questions.explanation: Scripts are just the same shell commands saved in a file.

questions.prompt: A script that only prints to the screen is fine for a job that runs at 3am from cron.
questions.explanation: Nobody is watching, so the output has to go somewhere you can read later.

questions.prompt: How would a script check whether a process is running?
options: Search the process list for its name
questions.explanation: It uses the same process tools you learned on day 16 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: Why check before starting a service?
options: To avoid starting a second copy of something already running
questions.explanation: Blindly starting things is how you end up with port conflicts and duplicate processes.

questions.prompt: What does the ampersand at the end of a command do?
questions.explanation: The script continues immediately instead of waiting.

questions.prompt: What does wait do in a script?
questions.explanation: It is how you run things in parallel and still know when they are all done.

questions.prompt: Why run several commands in parallel?
options: To finish faster when the tasks do not depend on each other
questions.explanation: Independent work does not need to be sequential.

questions.prompt: How would a script check whether nginx is active?
options: Use systemctl inside an if statement
questions.explanation: This connects directly to the systemd work from day 18 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: Why should a status script print one clear line?
options: So a human can understand the result at a glance
questions.explanation: A wall of output is a script that nobody will actually use.

questions.prompt: How would you count matches when searching a log?
options: Use grep with the count flag
Use wc on the whole file
questions.explanation: grep can count directly, which is simpler and faster than looping.

questions.prompt: Why warn only when a count passes a threshold?
options: Because a few errors are normal and constant alerts get ignored
questions.explanation: This is the same alert noise problem that applies to real monitoring.

questions.prompt: Why check whether a package is installed before installing it?
options: To avoid unnecessary work and make the script safe to run twice
questions.explanation: A script safe to run repeatedly is far more useful than one that only works once.

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of looping over a list of packages?
options: One script handles any number of packages instead of repeating yourself
questions.explanation: Adding a package becomes one line in a list, not a new block of code.

questions.prompt: Why should a script that manages services report what it did?
options: So you can tell afterwards whether it acted or found nothing to do
questions.explanation: Silence leaves you guessing whether it ran at all.

questions.prompt: A script that can be run twice without causing harm is more useful than one that cannot.
questions.explanation: Automation reruns constantly, and scripts that only work once cause real damage.

questions.prompt: Scripting systemd checks builds directly on what you learned about services in the Linux month.
questions.explanation: The second track is mostly automating what the first track just taught you.

questions.prompt: Alerting on every single error in a log is good practice.
questions.explanation: Constant alerts get ignored, which is the same noise problem real monitoring teams face.

questions.prompt: Why check disk usage as a plain number rather than reading the full output?
options: So the script can compare it against a threshold
questions.explanation: A script needs a value it can test, not text a human reads.

questions.prompt: What should a backup script do if the source folder does not exist?
questions.explanation: Backing up the wrong thing is worse than not backing up at all.

questions.prompt: Why delete archives older than a set number of days?
options: Because backups accumulate and fill the disk
questions.explanation: Unmanaged backups are a common cause of a full disk in production.

questions.prompt: Why give an environment variable a default value in a script?
options: So the script still works when the variable is not set
questions.explanation: Defaults make a script usable without a long setup process.

questions.prompt: Why move settings into a separate config file?
options: So you can change behaviour without editing the script
questions.explanation: It is the same principle as keeping configuration out of a container image.

questions.prompt: Why do cron jobs often fail when the same script works in your terminal?
options: Cron has a minimal environment, especially PATH
Cron runs as a different user only
questions.explanation: Full paths are usually the fix, which matches day 24 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What does the set command with the e flag do?
options: Exits the script when a command fails
questions.explanation: It stops the script continuing after a failure it should not ignore.

questions.prompt: What does the set command with the u flag do?
options: Treats an unset variable as an error
questions.explanation: It catches typos in variable names that would otherwise expand to nothing.

questions.prompt: Why quote every variable in a script?
options: So filenames with spaces do not break the command
questions.explanation: An unquoted variable containing a space is read as multiple arguments.

questions.prompt: What does shellcheck do?
options: Analyses it and reports likely bugs and bad practices
questions.explanation: It catches the common mistakes before they cause a problem in production.

questions.prompt: Why should a cron job write a line to a log every run?
options: So you can tell whether it ran, and when
questions.explanation: Without a record you cannot distinguish a job that did nothing from one that never ran.

questions.prompt: What makes a script worth keeping?
options: It does one real job reliably and tells you what happened
questions.explanation: Small, reliable and clear beats clever every time.

questions.prompt: An unquoted variable holding a filename with a space will be treated as two arguments.
questions.explanation: It is one of the most common bugs in shell scripts and quoting prevents it.

questions.prompt: Fixing every shellcheck warning is a reasonable standard for a script you intend to keep.
questions.explanation: Most of its warnings are real bugs waiting to happen rather than style opinions.

questions.prompt: A script written for your terminal will always work unchanged under cron.
questions.explanation: The environment differs, and PATH problems are the usual cause of the failure.
